frase_gancho.texto: A miniature temple where the image of the National Coat of Arms is born.

puente_narrativo.texto: On this stone, the eagle no longer holds a serpent, but war itself. Step up to an enormous stone drum where a king grips fifteen defeated chiefs by the hair.

guion_corto.texto: This is the Teocalli of the Sacred War, a miniature temple carved from a single block of basalt, a little over a meter tall. Researchers agree that it served as the ceremonial throne of Moctezuma Xocoyotzin. On the front it has the stairway of a temple; above, the disk of the Sun and two figures piercing their ears to draw blood: the god Huitzilopochtli and Moctezuma himself. The most famous side is the back: an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus that sprouts from the body of the Earth. Look at the beak: it does not hold a serpent, but a symbol, the atl-tlachinolli, «burnt water», the words the Mexica used for «war».

guion_largo.texto:
If you could walk around to the other side of this stone, you would discover the image you saw on the facade of the museum and that appears on the flag of Mexico. A golden eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, which sprouts from a stone figure, the Earth, whom you already know. The legend tells that the god Huitzilopochtli ordered his people to keep walking until they saw an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus. There they were to found their city. And they saw it on a small island in Lake Texcoco, in the year 2 House, which translates to 1325.

But look at the beak. On the modern coat of arms, the eagle devours a serpent. Not here. From its beak comes a double scroll, which splits into two streams: one of water and one of fire. It is the glyph atl-tlachinolli, «burnt water», which is a very Mexica way of saying «war». What seem to be opposites, water and fire, become a single word. Historians point out that the oldest images of the eagle and the prickly pear cactus had no serpent; that version came later.

Now raise your eyes to the top, to the sanctuary of the miniature temple. Between the two figures there is a solar disk, the sign Nahui Ollin, «Four Movement», the same one you will see on the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). On the left is Huitzilopochtli, with his hummingbird helmet; on the right, the tlatoani Moctezuma Xocoyotzin. Both pierce their ears with a thorn to offer their blood to the Sun. It is an important detail: the king and the god do the same thing. Even the powerful paid their share.

Count the dates as well. One of them is 2 Reed, the year 1507, when the Mexica celebrated the New Fire, the ceremony held every fifty-two years that you already know: putting out all the fires and lighting a new one. It was the last New Fire the Mexica lived to see; the next would have fallen in 1559, but by then the empire had fallen. This miniature temple marks the last great cycle before the end.

On the sides there are more gods. You can recognize Tláloc, the god of rain; Xiuhtecuhtli, the Lord of Fire, the same Old God you saw in stone and in clay; [Xochipilli](mna_s06_xochipilli), the god of flowers, whom you will see shortly; and Tlahuizcalpantecuhtli, the Lord of the Dawn, the planet Venus that was worshipped in Tula. The Teocalli is a kind of summary of the pantheon.

Its modern history is quite curious. It was found beneath the foundations of the National Palace, and was taken out in 1926. The National Palace stands on what were once the palaces of Moctezuma, and that is why so many pieces have turned up there. Who knows how many more sleep beneath its walls.

And there is something more. When you take out a peso coin and look at the reverse, you will see the eagle and the prickly pear cactus at its center. Five centuries later, that image is still seen every day. The Teocalli reminds you that the national emblem was not invented in an office: it came from a stone, from a myth, and from a foundation on the water.

texto: Count the steps of the stairway
Find the two figures piercing their ears to draw blood next to the disk of the Sun
Walk around and find the eagle on the prickly pear cactus: what comes out of its beak?

texto.Dimensions: 123 cm high x 92 cm wide x 100 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: On the Mexica coat of arms, the eagle always devoured a serpent.
texto.respuesta: Reality: On this stone, the symbol of war comes out of its beak, not a serpent; according to several historians, the serpent became popular in later versions of the emblem.
